code.title: Bitmask DP: cheapest worker-to-job assignment, with the chosen jobs rebuilt
code.python:
cost = [[9, 2, 7, 8], [6, 4, 3, 7], [5, 8, 1, 8], [7, 6, 9, 4]]
n = len(cost)
full = (1 << n) - 1
INF = 10**9
for i in range(n):
    print("worker " + str(i) + " costs: " + " ".join(map(str, cost[i])))

dp = [INF] * (1 << n)     # dp[mask] = cheapest way to hand out the jobs in mask
last = [0] * (1 << n)     # last[mask] = job handed out most recently
dp[0] = 0
for mask in range(full):
    w = bin(mask).count("1")          # the next worker is the number of jobs taken
    for j in range(n):
        if mask >> j & 1:             # job j is already taken
            continue
        nm = mask | (1 << j)
        if dp[mask] + cost[w][j] < dp[nm]:
            dp[nm] = dp[mask] + cost[w][j]
            last[nm] = j
print("Minimum total cost = " + str(dp[full]))

job = [0] * n
mask = full
while mask:                           # walk back through the choices
    job[bin(mask).count("1") - 1] = last[mask]
    mask ^= 1 << last[mask]
for i in range(n):
    print("worker " + str(i) + " -> job " + str(job[i]) + " (cost " + str(cost[i][job[i]]) + ")")
# Time O(2^n * n), space O(2^n)

followUps:
With n = 40 a table of 240 subsets is about a trillion entries, so you split the items into two halves of 20 and list the 220 (about one million) subsets of each half separately. This is called meet in the middle.

Example, subset sum with target 50: store every sum of the left half in a sorted list; for each sum s of the right half, binary-search for 50 − s on the left. If the left half can make 20 and the right half can make 30, you have found a hit.

Cost: O(2n/2 · n) time and O(2n/2) memory, roughly 20 million steps instead of a trillion. It only works when the two halves combine through a simple lookup (a sum, an XOR, a count). It does not rescue an order-dependent problem such as TSP.

Remember, for every state, which choice produced its best value, then walk backwards from the final state to the start.

  1. While filling the table, whenever a transition improves dp[newMask], also write last[newMask] = j (the item just added). For TSP store the previous city in par[mask][v].
  2. Start at the full mask, read the stored item, remove its bit, and repeat until the mask is 0.
  3. You collected the order from last to first, so reverse it.
int mask = full;
while (mask != 0) {
    order.add(last[mask]);
    mask ^= 1 << last[mask];
}
Collections.reverse(order);

Example: full = 1111, last = 3, then 0111 with last = 2, and so on. The walk takes O(n) steps and the extra table costs the same memory as dp.

code.title: Held-Karp: shortest round trip through 4 cities with dp[mask][last city]
code.python:
d = [[0, 10, 15, 20], [10, 0, 35, 25], [15, 35, 0, 30], [20, 25, 30, 0]]
n = len(d)
full = (1 << n) - 1
INF = 10**9
for i in range(n):
    print("from city " + str(i) + ": " + " ".join(map(str, d[i])))

# dp[mask][v] = cheapest path that starts at city 0, visits exactly mask, ends at v
dp = [[INF] * n for _ in range(1 << n)]
dp[1][0] = 0                              # only city 0 visited, standing on it
for mask in range(1, full + 1):
    for v in range(n):
        if dp[mask][v] == INF:
            continue
        for u in range(n):                # extend the path by one unvisited city
            if mask >> u & 1:
                continue
            nm = mask | (1 << u)
            dp[nm][u] = min(dp[nm][u], dp[mask][v] + d[v][u])

best = INF
for v in range(1, n):                     # close the tour back to city 0
    best = min(best, dp[full][v] + d[v][0])
print("States = " + str((1 << n) * n) + ", shortest tour = " + str(best))
# Time O(2^n * n^2), space O(2^n * n)

followUps:
Store the earliest time you can be at city v after visiting the set mask, and throw away any move that arrives after the city's closing time.

If the goal is to finish as early as possible, dp[mask][v] = earliest arrival. The transition to city u is t = max(dp[mask][v] + travel[v][u], open[u]) (you wait if you are early), and it is allowed only if t ≤ close[u]. Arriving earlier is never worse, so one number per state is enough and the cost stays O(2n·n2).

Example: you reach B at time 7, its window is [10, 12], so you wait until 10. If you would reach it at 13, that move is dropped.

If cost and time are different things (cheapest fuel but still on time), one number is not enough: add time to the state or keep a list of non-dominated (cost, time) pairs per state, which is much heavier.

Fix city 0 as the start and leave its bit out of the mask, because it is in every state anyway. The mask then covers only the other n − 1 cities, which halves the number of masks.

Numbers for n = 20 with 4-byte ints: 220 · 20 · 4 bytes ≈ 84 MB before, 219 · 19 · 4 bytes ≈ 40 MB after. Time also halves.

Other savings that stack on top:

  • Use int (or even short) instead of long when the tour length fits.
  • Use one flat array indexed mask * n + v instead of an array of arrays.
  • Process masks by number of set bits and keep only two neighbouring layers. That saves the most, but you lose easy path reconstruction.

code.title: Digit DP with tight and started flags: count numbers in [0, N] with no repeated digit

followUps:
Fill the memo once and never clear it, which is safe as long as the memo key does not depend on N.

Two rules make that true:

  • Store only non-tight states. A free state means "the remaining digits can be anything", so its count is the same for every N.
  • Index the position by digits remaining, not by position from the left. "3 digits left, digit sum so far 5" means the same thing for N = 4821 and for N = 97310; "position 2" does not.

Each query then only walks the single tight chain: at each of its 18 positions it tries up to 10 digits and reads a ready memo entry. That is about 180 lookups per query, so 105 queries cost about 2·107 steps plus one fill of the table.

Use an iterative digit DP over the string with answers taken modulo a prime, and avoid computing L − 1 by checking L itself separately.

  • No recursion: 105 levels of recursion overflows the stack. Loop over positions and keep only two rows: the counts for the free states, plus one single tight state.
  • Small state: for example the digit sum modulo m. Work is O(length · states · 10); with m = 100 that is 105 · 100 · 10 = 108 simple steps and O(states) memory.
  • Range: answer = count(R) − count(L) + (1 if L itself is valid), all mod p, adding p before the final % so it is not negative. Subtracting 1 from a 105-digit string works too, but the borrow and a possible leading zero are easy to get wrong.

code.title: K-th smallest number with digit sum S, by counting and descending digit by digit
code.python:
LEN = 18
S = 10
# ways[len][s] = digit strings of this length (zeros allowed) with sum s
ways = [[0] * (S + 1) for _ in range(LEN + 1)]
ways[0][0] = 1
for length in range(1, LEN + 1):
    for s in range(S + 1):
        for d in range(min(9, s) + 1):
            ways[length][s] += ways[length - 1][s - d]

def kth(k, S):
    length = 1
    while True:                              # step 1: find how many digits the answer has
        cnt = sum(ways[length - 1][S - d] for d in range(1, min(9, S) + 1))
        if k <= cnt:
            break
        k -= cnt                             # skip every number of this length
        length += 1
    out = []
    rem = S
    for pos in range(length):                # step 2: fix the digits from left to right
        for d in range(1 if pos == 0 else 0, min(9, rem) + 1):
            c = ways[length - pos - 1][rem - d]   # numbers that start with this prefix
            if k <= c:
                out.append(str(d))
                rem -= d
                break
            k -= c                           # the answer is not under digit d
    return "".join(out)

for k in [1, 5, 9, 10, 20, 100, 1000]:
    print("S = " + str(S) + ", K = " + str(k) + " -> " + kth(k, S))
# Time O(digits * 10) per query after an O(digits * S * 10) table; space O(digits * S)

followUps:
The upper bound does not change which number is K-th, it only decides whether a K-th number exists. The numbers with digit sum S that are ≤ N are simply the first few entries of the full sorted list.

  1. Run a normal digit DP with the tight flag to get total = how many numbers in [1, N] have digit sum S.
  2. If K > total, report that there is no answer.
  3. Otherwise run the unbounded K-th search exactly as before.

Example with S = 10 and N = 50: the list is 19, 28, 37, 46, so total = 4. K = 3 gives 37; K = 5 (which would be 55) does not exist.

A lower bound L works the same way: add the count of valid numbers below L to K first. Cost: one extra digit DP, O(digits · S · 10).

Compare it with a brute force on small inputs, and check a few facts that must always hold.

  • Brute force: loop x = 1, 2, 3, … and keep those whose digits add up to S; the K-th one kept is the expected answer. For S = 10 the list starts 19, 28, 37, 46, 55, 64, 73, 82, 91, 109, so K = 10 must give 109. Run this for every S ≤ 20 and K ≤ 2000.
  • Digit sum: the digits of every answer must add up to exactly S.
  • Order: the answer for K + 1 must be strictly larger than the answer for K.
  • Round trip: counting the numbers ≤ answer with digit sum S (by a separate digit DP) must return K.
  • Edges: K = 1, S = 1 (1, 10, 100, …), S = 9 · digits, and a K so large that the count needs 64-bit integers.

code.title: Forward push for a probability, backward pull for an expected value (random +1/+2 walk)
code.python:
n = 10
print("Walk from 0; each step is +1 or +2 with probability 1/2; target n = " + str(n))

# Forward: the probability is known at the start (1 at position 0), so push it along.
p = [0.0] * (n + 2)
p[0] = 1.0
for i in range(n):
    p[i + 1] += p[i] * 0.5
    p[i + 2] += p[i] * 0.5
print("P(land exactly on %d) = %.4f" % (n, p[n]))

# Backward: the expected remaining steps are known at the end (0 once we reach n).
e = [0.0] * (n + 2)
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    e[i] = 1 + 0.5 * e[i + 1] + 0.5 * e[i + 2]   # one step now, then the average future
print("E(steps until position >= %d) = %.4f" % (n, e[0]))

for i in range(0, n + 1, 4):
    print("position %d: P(visit) = %.4f, E(steps left) = %.4f" % (i, p[i], e[i]))
# Time O(n), space O(n)

followUps:
With 300 states that can loop back to each other, write one linear equation per state and solve them all together with Gaussian elimination.

Each state gives E[s] = cost + Σ p · E[next], with E = 0 at the goal. That is 300 equations in 300 unknowns; elimination costs about 3003 = 2.7·107 operations and 3002 numbers of memory, which is fast.

Tiny example with two states: E0 = 1 + 0.5·E0 + 0.5·E1 and E1 = 1 + 0.5·E0 (the other half reaches the goal). Substituting gives 0.25·E0 = 1.5, so E0 = 6 and E1 = 4.

Use doubles with partial pivoting (swap in the row with the largest pivot), or modular inverses if the answer is wanted mod a prime. Repeating the update until the values stop changing also works, but it can converge slowly.

Monte-Carlo (simulate the process many times and average) is fine when an approximate answer is enough, and it is always fine as a second opinion on your exact DP.

The error shrinks only like 1/√trials. With 106 runs the average is off by about (standard deviation)/1000, so you get roughly 3 correct decimals. To get 6 decimals you would need about 1012 runs.

  • Acceptable: checking a DP during testing (the DP says 6.0, the simulation says 5.998); estimating a system whose state space is far too large for a table; product questions where ±1% is good enough.
  • Not acceptable: a judge that wants an error of 10−6 or an exact fraction modulo a prime; very rare events (probability 10−9 will almost never show up in a sample).

Fix the random seed so the result can be reproduced.

code.title: Linearity of expectation: average number of fixed points is 1, checked over all permutations
code.python:
def gen(pos, fixed, n, used, totals):
    # Place a value at every position; 'fixed' counts positions where value == position.
    if pos == n:
        totals[0] += 1
        totals[1] += fixed
        return
    for v in range(n):
        if used[v]:
            continue
        used[v] = True
        gen(pos + 1, fixed + (1 if v == pos else 0), n, used, totals)
        used[v] = False

for n in range(3, 8):
    totals = [0, 0]                      # [number of permutations, total fixed points]
    gen(0, 0, n, [False] * n, totals)    # brute force: O(n!) work
    # Linearity: each of the n cards stays put with probability 1/n, so E = n * (1/n) = 1.
    print("n = " + str(n) + ": " + str(totals[0]) + " permutations, " + str(totals[1])
          + " fixed points in total, average = " + str(totals[1] // totals[0]) + " (formula n * 1/n = 1)")
# Brute force: time O(n * n!), space O(n). Formula: O(1).

followUps:
The expected number of inversions in a random permutation of n items is n(n − 1)/4.

An inversion is a pair of positions i < j where the earlier value is larger. Give every pair its own indicator: it is 1 if the pair is inverted, else 0. In a random permutation the two values of a pair are equally likely to be in either order, so each indicator has expectation 1/2. There are n(n − 1)/2 pairs, and expectations add even though the pairs are not independent, so the total is n(n − 1)/2 · 1/2.

Check with n = 3: the six permutations have 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 inversions, total 9, average 1.5, and 3·2/4 = 1.5. For n = 4 the formula gives 3.

Cost: O(1), with no DP over permutations at all.

To collect all n different coupons you need on average n · (1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/n) draws, which is about n · ln n.

Split the wait into n stages. When you already own i different coupons, a draw is new with probability (n − i)/n, so that stage takes n/(n − i) draws on average. The total wait is the sum of the stage waits, and expectations simply add: n/n + n/(n − 1) + … + n/1.

Example with n = 3: 3/3 + 3/2 + 3/1 = 1 + 1.5 + 3 = 5.5 draws. For n = 100 it is about 519 draws.

Computing it is one loop, O(n) time and O(1) space. A DP over "which coupons do I own" would need 2n states.

code.title: dp[i] = a[i] + max of the last k dp values: O(N*k) loop vs O(N) monotonic deque
code.python:
def slow(a, k):                       # try every allowed j: O(N * k)
    n = len(a)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = a[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[j] for j in range(max(0, i - k), i))
    return dp[n - 1]

def fast(a, k):                       # same recurrence, the max comes from a deque
    n = len(a)
    dp = [0] * n
    dq = [0] * n                      # dq holds indices, their dp values decrease
    head, tail = 0, 0
    dp[0] = a[0]
    dq[tail] = 0
    tail += 1
    for i in range(1, n):
        if dq[head] < i - k:          # the front left the window
            head += 1
        dp[i] = a[i] + dp[dq[head]]   # the front is the window maximum
        while tail > head and dp[dq[tail - 1]] <= dp[i]:   # drop values that can never win
            tail -= 1
        dq[tail] = i
        tail += 1
    return dp[n - 1]

a = [1, -5, -20, 4, -1, 3, -6, -3]
k = 2
print("a = " + " ".join(map(str, a)) + ", jump at most k = " + str(k))
print("O(N*k) loop: best score = " + str(slow(a, k)))
print("O(N) deque:  best score = " + str(fast(a, k)))
# Deque version: time O(N) (each index is pushed and popped once), space O(N)

followUps:
You cannot use a max-Fenwick tree when a stored value may get smaller or be removed, or when you need the maximum of a middle range [l, r] instead of a prefix [1, r].

A Fenwick tree for sums answers a range as prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1), because addition can be undone. Maximum cannot be undone. Example: position 2 holds 5 and position 4 holds 3. The prefix maxima are max[1..2] = 5 and max[1..4] = 5; from those two numbers you cannot recover max[3..4] = 3. In the same way, if position 2 is lowered from 5 to 1, the nodes that already absorbed the 5 cannot tell what their new maximum is.

So a max-Fenwick is safe only for "point update that only raises a value, plus prefix query", as in LIS. For anything else use a segment tree: any range and any update in O(log N), with about 2N to 4N memory.

Index order comes for free from the array, so you remove the second condition with divide and conquer on the index and the third with a Fenwick tree. This is CDQ divide and conquer.

  1. Split the index range [l, r] at mid and solve the left half first, so its dp values are final.
  2. Cross step: sort the left half and the right half by a. Sweep the right half in increasing a; before handling element i, insert into a max-Fenwick (keyed by b) every left element with a[j] < a[i]. Then dp[i] = max(dp[i], 1 + query(b[i] − 1)).
  3. Clear the Fenwick tree by undoing only the positions you touched, then solve the right half.

The order left, cross, right matters, because the right half needs finished values from the left. Cost: O(N log2 N) time and O(N) memory, instead of O(N2).

code.title: Convex hull trick with a monotone deque: split an array into groups, cost (sum)^2 + C
code.python:
M = []          # line j: y = M[j] * x + B[j]
B = []
head = 0

def useless(l1, l2, m3, b3):
    # With slopes decreasing, the middle line l2 is never the minimum if l3 overtakes l1 before l2 does.
    return (b3 - B[l1]) * (M[l1] - M[l2]) <= (B[l2] - B[l1]) * (M[l1] - m3)

def add(m, b):
    while len(M) - head >= 2 and useless(len(M) - 2, len(M) - 1, m, b):
        M.pop()
        B.pop()
    M.append(m)
    B.append(b)

def query(x):   # x only grows, so the front pointer only moves forward
    global head
    while len(M) - head >= 2 and M[head + 1] * x + B[head + 1] <= M[head] * x + B[head]:
        head += 1
    return M[head] * x + B[head]

a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
C = 20
n = len(a)
p = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    p[i + 1] = p[i] + a[i]

slow = [0] * (n + 1)                      # plain O(N^2) reference
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    slow[i] = min(slow[j] + (p[i] - p[j]) ** 2 + C for j in range(i))

# (p[i]-p[j])^2 = p[i]^2 - 2*p[j]*p[i] + p[j]^2  ->  line with slope -2*p[j], intercept dp[j]+p[j]^2
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
add(0, 0)
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    dp[i] = query(p[i]) + p[i] * p[i] + C
    add(-2 * p[i], dp[i] + p[i] * p[i])

print("a = " + " ".join(map(str, a)) + ", cost per group = (sum)^2 + " + str(C))
print("O(N^2) DP:         " + str(slow[n]))
print("Convex hull trick: " + str(dp[n]))
# Time O(N), space O(N)

followUps:
It compares the new line with the line stored in the current node at the middle x of that node, keeps the better one there, and pushes the loser down into the one half where it can still win.

Example on x in [0, 15], minimum wanted. The root holds y = 3x. Insert y = −2x + 40:

  • At mid = 7: 3·7 = 21 against −14 + 40 = 26. The old line wins and stays in the root.
  • The loser is better at the right end (x = 15: 10 against 45), so it goes into the right child [8, 15] and the same test repeats there.

Two straight lines cross at most once, so the loser can be better on only one side of mid; that is why only one child is visited. Each insert and each query walks one root-to-leaf path: O(log C) time, where C is the size of the x range, and O(C) memory (or O(number of lines) with nodes created on demand).

Two lines with the same slope are parallel and never cross, so keep only the better one: the smaller intercept for a minimum, the larger for a maximum.

You must handle this before the usual "is the middle line useless" test, because the crossing point of two parallel lines means dividing by (m1 − m2) = 0, and the cross-multiplied form quietly gives a wrong answer instead.

if (size > 0 && M[size-1] == m) {
    if (B[size-1] <= b) return;  // old line is at least as good
    size--;                      // new line replaces it
}
// ...then the normal pop loop and push

Example: y = 2x + 5 is on the hull and y = 2x + 3 arrives. The new one is lower everywhere, so remove the old one and add the new one. If y = 2x + 9 arrives instead, ignore it. Cost stays O(1) amortised per line.

code.title: Li Chao tree: insert lines in any order, query the minimum at a point
code.python:
LO, HI = 0, 15
INF = 10**18
M = [0] * 64          # one line per segment-tree node
B = [INF] * 64        # every node starts with y = INF

def insert(node, lo, hi, m, b):
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if m * mid + b < M[node] * mid + B[node]:      # the line that wins at mid stays here
        M[node], m = m, M[node]
        B[node], b = b, B[node]
    if lo == hi:
        return
    # Two lines cross at most once, so the loser can win on one side only.
    if m * lo + b < M[node] * lo + B[node]:
        insert(2 * node, lo, mid, m, b)
    elif m * hi + b < M[node] * hi + B[node]:
        insert(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, m, b)

def query(x):                                      # best of the lines on the root-to-leaf path
    node, lo, hi = 1, LO, HI
    best = INF
    while True:
        best = min(best, M[node] * x + B[node])
        if lo == hi:
            return best
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if x <= mid:
            node, hi = 2 * node, mid
        else:
            node, lo = 2 * node + 1, mid + 1

lines = [(3, 0), (-2, 40), (0, 18), (1, 5)]
for m, b in lines:
    insert(1, LO, HI, m, b)
    print("insert y = " + str(m) + "x + " + str(b))
for x in [0, 4, 8, 12, 15]:
    brute = min(m * x + b for m, b in lines)
    print("x = " + str(x) + ": Li Chao min = " + str(query(x)) + ", brute force = " + str(brute))
# Time O(log C) per insert and per query, space O(C) for an x range of size C

followUps:
Cut the range [l, r] into the usual O(log C) segment-tree nodes, exactly like a range update, and run the normal Li Chao insert inside each of those nodes.

A node that lies fully inside [l, r] can treat the segment as a full line, because the segment is valid on the node's whole range. Nodes that only partly overlap are not given the line; you just recurse into their children.

Example on the domain [0, 15] with a segment valid on [3, 9]: it is inserted into the nodes [3, 3], [4, 7] and [8, 9]. A query at x = 2 never sees it, a query at x = 5 does.

Cost: O(log C) nodes, each with an O(log C) push-down, so O(log2 C) per segment. Queries are unchanged at O(log C). Memory is O(C), or O(segments · log C) with nodes created on demand.

Do not build the whole tree. Either create nodes only when an insert reaches them, or shrink the x range to just the query points.

  • Dynamic nodes: keep child pointers and start with a root for [0, 1018]. One insert walks about 60 levels and creates at most one new node, so memory is O(number of lines).
  • Offline compression: if all query x values are known up front, sort them and build the tree over their indices. With 105 queries the tree has 17 levels, and "mid" means the middle query point.

Two details matter at this size. Compute mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 so the sum does not overflow. And m · x can reach 109 · 1018 = 1027, which does not fit in 64 bits, so compare with a 128-bit type (__int128, Math.multiplyHigh, BigInteger) or prove smaller bounds.

code.title: Quadrangle inequality checked by brute force: (sum)^2 passes, -(length)^2 fails
code.python:
a = [2, 7, 1, 8, 2, 8]
n = len(a)
p = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    p[i + 1] = p[i] + a[i]

def w(kind, i, j):
    # kind 0: (sum of a[i..j])^2, a convex cost.  kind 1: -(length)^2, a concave cost.
    if kind == 0:
        s = p[j + 1] - p[i]
        return s * s
    length = j - i + 1
    return -length * length

def check(kind, name):
    checks, bad, first = 0, 0, ""
    for x in range(n):
        for y in range(x, n):
            for c in range(y, n):
                for d in range(c, n):              # every x <= y <= c <= d
                    crossing = w(kind, x, c) + w(kind, y, d)
                    nested = w(kind, x, d) + w(kind, y, c)
                    checks += 1
                    if crossing > nested:          # QI demands crossing <= nested
                        if bad == 0:
                            first = (", first: a=" + str(x) + " b=" + str(y) + " c=" + str(c) + " d=" + str(d)
                                     + " gives " + str(crossing) + " > " + str(nested))
                        bad += 1
    print(name + ": " + str(bad) + " violations in " + str(checks) + " checks" + first)

print("a = " + " ".join(map(str, a)))
check(0, "w = (sum)^2")
check(1, "w = -(length)^2")
# Time O(N^4) for the full check, space O(N)

followUps:
Any cost that grows more and more slowly with the length of the interval breaks it, for example w(i, j) = sqrt(j − i) or w(i, j) = −(j − i)2.

Take the second one with a = 0, b = 1, c = 2, d = 3. The crossing pair costs w(0, 2) + w(1, 3) = −4 − 4 = −8. The nested pair costs w(0, 3) + w(1, 2) = −9 − 1 = −10. The inequality needs −8 ≤ −10, which is false.

In words: such a cost rewards one very long interval plus one very short one over two medium ones, which is the opposite of what QI promises. Then the best split point can jump backwards as i grows, and D&C or Knuth optimisation returns a wrong answer without any crash. Other common offenders are costs with a maximum or a count of distinct values multiplied by something non-monotone. For these you fall back to the plain DP or a different technique.

Test the short "neighbour" form of the inequality on many small random arrays, and separately check that the best split points of the slow DP never move backwards.

It is enough to check w(i, j) + w(i+1, j+1) ≤ w(i, j+1) + w(i+1, j) for all i < j. If this holds for every neighbouring pair, the general four-index version follows by adding these up, so you need O(N2) checks instead of O(N4).

for (int i = 0; i + 1 < n; i++)
  for (int j = i + 1; j + 1 < n; j++)
    if (w(i,j) + w(i+1,j+1) > w(i,j+1) + w(i+1,j))
      report(i, j);

Run it on a few thousand arrays of length 8 with values 0..5, including zeros and equal values. One counterexample proves the property is false; passing proves nothing formally, but it is strong evidence. Also print opt[i] from the O(N2) DP and assert opt[i] ≤ opt[i+1].

code.title: Divide and conquer optimisation: split into K groups, plain O(K*N^2) vs O(K*N log N)
code.python:
INF = 10**15
a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
n, K = len(a), 3
p = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    p[i + 1] = p[i] + a[i]

def cost(j, i):                       # group a[j..i-1]
    return (p[i] - p[j]) ** 2

def solve(lo, hi, opt_lo, opt_hi, prev, cur):
    # Fill cur[lo..hi]; the best split for each of them lies in [opt_lo, opt_hi].
    if lo > hi:
        return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    best, best_j = None, opt_lo
    for j in range(opt_lo, min(mid - 1, opt_hi) + 1):
        v = prev[j] + cost(j, mid)
        if best is None or v < best:
            best, best_j = v, j
    cur[mid] = best
    solve(lo, mid - 1, opt_lo, best_j, prev, cur)   # smaller i -> split point no further right
    solve(mid + 1, hi, best_j, opt_hi, prev, cur)   # larger i  -> split point no further left

slow = [[INF] * (n + 1) for _ in range(K + 1)]      # slow[k][i]: first i items in k groups
slow[0][0] = 0
for k in range(1, K + 1):
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(i):
            slow[k][i] = min(slow[k][i], slow[k - 1][j] + cost(j, i))

prev = [INF] * (n + 1)
prev[0] = 0
for k in range(1, K + 1):                           # one layer per group count
    cur = [INF] * (n + 1)
    solve(1, n, 0, n - 1, prev, cur)
    prev = cur

print("a = " + " ".join(map(str, a)) + ", K = " + str(K) + " groups, cost of a group = (sum)^2")
print("Plain DP O(K*N^2):       " + str(slow[K][n]))
print("D&C opt O(K*N log N):    " + str(prev[n]))
# Time O(K * N log N), space O(N) for the optimised version

followUps:
You do not force the inner DP to use exactly K groups; you find the penalty λ where K is one of the optimal group counts and then subtract λ · K yourself.

With ties, a single λ can be optimal for a whole range of group counts, for example 3, 4, 5 and 6, and the DP reports just one of them. So:

  1. Break ties in one fixed direction, for example always prefer fewer groups when values are equal.
  2. Binary-search for the smallest λ whose reported count is ≤ K.
  3. Answer = f(λ) − λ · K, using the K you want, not the count the DP returned.

Example: at λ = 7 the penalised optimum is f = 100 and the DP reports 3 groups, but 5 is also optimal there. For K = 5 the answer is 100 − 7·5 = 65.

This is valid because all those counts lie on one straight piece of the convex curve. With integer costs an integer λ is enough. Rebuilding the actual groups for exactly K needs extra work.

Yes, but usually you choose one of them; they are combined mainly when the lines do not arrive in sorted slope order.

  • Layered K-group DP with a line-shaped cost: plain CHT per layer already gives O(K·N), which beats D&C optimisation's O(K·N log N). Use D&C optimisation when the cost satisfies the quadrangle inequality but cannot be written as slope × x + intercept.
  • Real combination (CDQ + CHT): for a 1D DP whose slopes and queries are in random order, split the indices in half, solve the left half, sort its lines by slope and the right half's queries by x, and sweep with the O(N) monotone hull; then solve the right half. That is O(N log2 N), an offline alternative to a Li Chao tree.

Example: dp[i] = min(dp[j] + b[j]·a[i]) with unsorted a and b needs either Li Chao (O(N log N)) or this CDQ + CHT scheme.

code.title: SOS DP: count pairs with a[i] & a[j] == 0, checked against the O(N^2) loop
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 0, 6, 7, 2, 0]
B = 3
FULL = (1 << B) - 1
print("a = " + " ".join(map(str, a)) + " (values below 2^" + str(B) + ")")

brute = 0                                  # O(N^2) reference
for x in a:
    for y in a:
        if x & y == 0:
            brute += 1

f = [0] * (1 << B)                         # f[mask] starts as "how many values equal mask"
for x in a:
    f[x] += 1
zeros = f[0]
for bit in range(B):                       # one bit at a time: a prefix sum per dimension
    for mask in range(FULL + 1):
        if mask >> bit & 1:
            f[mask] += f[mask ^ (1 << bit)]
# Now f[mask] = how many values are submasks of mask.

ordered = 0
for x in a:
    ordered += f[FULL ^ x]                 # partners must fit inside the complement of x
print("Ordered pairs, brute force: " + str(brute))
print("Ordered pairs, SOS DP:      " + str(ordered))
print("Unordered pairs i < j:      " + str((ordered - zeros) // 2))
# Time O(B * 2^B + N), space O(2^B)

followUps:
Take the ordered count, subtract the pairs of an element with itself, and divide by two: unordered = (ordered − zeros) / 2, where zeros is the number of elements equal to 0.

The ordered count includes (i, j) and (j, i) separately, so every real pair is counted twice. It also includes (i, i), and a[i] & a[i] = a[i] is 0 only when a[i] = 0, so exactly zeros such self-pairs are in the total.

Example: a = [1, 2, 0]. Ordered pairs with AND 0: (1,2), (2,1), (1,0), (0,1), (2,0), (0,2), (0,0) = 7. One zero, so (7 − 1) / 2 = 3, which matches the three pairs {1,2}, {1,0}, {2,0}.

The extra work is O(1) after the SOS pass. Use 64-bit integers: with N = 106 the count can reach about 1012.

Count pairs whose OR fits inside X using SOS, then turn "inside X" into "exactly X" by running the same loops with a minus sign.

  1. F[X] = number of elements that are submasks of X (ordinary SOS over the frequency array).
  2. G[X] = F[X] · F[X]: both elements fit inside X, so their OR does too.
  3. Inverse SOS on G: for each bit, for each mask with that bit, G[mask] −= G[mask ^ bit]. Now G[X] is the number of ordered pairs with OR exactly X.
for (int b = 0; b < B; b++)
  for (int m = 0; m < (1 << B); m++)
    if ((m >> b & 1) == 1) G[m] -= G[m ^ (1 << b)];

Example a = [1, 2, 3]: F[3] = 3 so G[3] = 9, G[1] = G[2] = 1, G[0] = 0. Exact count for 3 is 9 − 1 − 1 + 0 = 7: all nine ordered pairs except (1,1) and (2,2). Cost O(B · 2B) time, O(2B) space.

code.title: Random stress test: a fast DP against a brute force, and how it exposes a bug
code.python:
seed = 1

def nxt():                                 # tiny repeatable random generator
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 75 + 74) % 65537
    return seed

def brute(a):                              # obviously correct: try every subarray, O(n^2)
    best = a[0]
    for i in range(len(a)):
        s = 0
        for j in range(i, len(a)):
            s += a[j]
            best = max(best, s)
    return best

def kadane(a, buggy):                      # fast DP, O(n); the buggy version starts best at 0
    cur = 0
    best = 0 if buggy else a[0]
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def stress(name, buggy):
    global seed
    seed = 1                               # fixed seed: the same cases on every run
    for t in range(1, 1001):
        n = nxt() % 6 + 1                  # tiny sizes and tiny values force ties and edge cases
        a = [nxt() % 11 - 5 for _ in range(n)]
        want, got = brute(a), kadane(a, buggy)
        if want != got:
            print(name + ": case " + str(t) + " FAILED, input = " + " ".join(map(str, a))
                  + ", expected " + str(want) + ", got " + str(got))
            return
    print(name + ": all 1000 random cases passed")

print("Maximum subarray sum: fast DP compared with brute force")
stress("correct version", False)
stress("buggy version (best starts at 0)", True)
# Each case: O(n^2) for the reference, O(n) for the fast version

followUps:
Make the generator produce tiny inputs in the first place, then keep deleting and lowering parts of the failing input for as long as the two programs still disagree.

  1. Generate small: n from 1 to 5 and values from 0 to 3. Run many cases and keep the failing one with the fewest elements instead of stopping at the first.
  2. Delete: try removing each element (or each half) in turn; if the outputs still differ, keep the shorter input.
  3. Simplify values: try replacing each value by 0, 1, or half of itself; keep any change that still fails.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until nothing more can be changed.

Example: [4, −2, −5, 3, −1] fails. Dropping elements one at a time still fails down to [−1], which shows the bug at once: an all-negative array. Each attempt costs one run of both programs, so shrinking takes only a few dozen runs.

First work out the largest value any variable can reach, then feed the program the biggest allowed input and compare it with a version that cannot overflow.

  • Bound by hand: N = 105 values of 109 give a prefix sum of 1014; squaring it gives 1028, far above the 64-bit limit of about 9.2·1018. A product of two lines' terms in the CHT "useless" test is a typical place where this hides.
  • Max-value tests: all values at the maximum, n at the maximum, and K = 1 so one group holds everything. Random small tests never reach these sizes.
  • Wide reference: compare against Python integers, BigInteger, or __int128.
  • Let the tools shout: in Java use Math.addExact and Math.multiplyExact in a debug build; in C++ compile with -fsanitize=undefined, which reports signed overflow at the exact line.

A typical case: the assistant sped up a DP with the monotone-deque convex hull trick, but the query points were not increasing, so the front pointer skipped lines that were needed later.

The recurrence was dp[i] = min(dp[j] + (p[i] − p[j])2) + C over prefix sums p. The deque version assumes p only grows. The samples had positive numbers, so it passed. With a negative value, for example a = [3, −5, 4], the prefix sums are 3, −2, 2: they go down and then up, the slopes are no longer sorted, and the answer is wrong with no crash or warning.

A stress test against the O(N2) DP with values from −5 to 5 and n ≤ 6 found a failing input within the first few cases. The fix was a Li Chao tree, which needs no ordering, at O(N log N). The lesson is to ask "what does this optimisation assume?" before accepting it.

I would never hand over the decision that the solution is correct, because I am the one who answers for it.

In practice that means four things stay with me:

  • The state and the recurrence: what dp[i] means in one sentence. If I cannot say it, I cannot review the code.
  • The precondition check: are slopes really sorted, does the cost really satisfy the quadrangle inequality, is the answer really convex in K. For example, "values can be negative" in the statement silently kills the monotone deque.
  • The budget: 220 · 20 states times 8 bytes is 168 MB, which decides whether the approach is allowed at all.
  • The test plan and the final read-through: which edge cases exist and whether the reference is truly independent of the fast code.

Typing the template, writing the brute force and generating random cases are fine to delegate.
